summary: Describes how to send Vorbis-encoded audio in RTP, including packaging the raw data and delivering the decoder setup information such as codebooks. It also contains media type registrations and details for using Vorbis with SDP. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a shipping guide for sending music in the Vorbis format over the internet, including the instructions needed to play it.

questions: what is the vorbis rtp payload format
how to stream vorbis over rtp
what is the vorbis ident field
subtitle: How to chop Vorbis audio into RTP packets and get the decoder its setup data.

tldr.problem: Vorbis normally travels inside an Ogg stream and needs setup headers (codebooks) before any audio can be decoded, which is awkward over RTP's unreliable transport.
tldr.mechanism: Raw Vorbis packets go straight into RTP behind a 4-octet payload header with a 24-bit Ident, fragment type, data type and packet count; configuration is sent in the SDP or in-band.
tldr.outcome: Streams can carry up to 15 packets per payload, fragment large packets, and switch codebooks mid-session by changing the Ident.

today: RFC 5215 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the definition of this Vorbis RTP payload format.

sections.title: Vorbis over RTP
sections.content:
Vorbis is a general purpose perceptual audio codec built to scale over a wide range of bit rates. The text puts the high-quality end in the same league as MPEG-4 AAC, and says it supports sample rates from 8kHz to 192kHz and up to 255 discrete channels.

Vorbis is usually wrapped in an Ogg bitstream (RFC 3533) for framing and synchronization. RTP does not need that layer, so this payload format carries raw Vorbis packets instead. Requirement words follow BCP 14 (RFC 2119).
sections.plainLanguage: Vorbis shrinks music. Usually it travels in an Ogg box, but for live internet streaming the box is not needed, so the music goes out unboxed.

sections.title: RTP and Payload Headers
sections.content:
Each packet is the standard RTP header (RFC 3550), then a 4-octet payload header, then the payload data. An RTP payload MUST hold just one of three types of Vorbis data.

The RTP header is used as follows. Version is 2. The marker bit is set to zero because silence suppression is not used. The payload type is expected to come from an RTP profile, or be a dynamically allocated value. The timestamp is the sampling time of the first sample of the first Vorbis packet, and its clock frequency MUST equal the audio sample rate, conveyed out of band such as in SDP.

The payload header has four fields:

  • Ident (24 bits): ties the data to a decoding configuration, as a network byte order integer.
  • F, fragment type (2 bits): 0 not fragmented, 1 start, 2 continuation, 3 end.
  • VDT, Vorbis data type (2 bits): 0 raw payload, 1 packed configuration, 2 legacy comment, 3 reserved. Packets with VDT 3 MUST be ignored.
  • The last 4 bits: the number of complete packets in the payload, at most 15. For fragmented data it MUST be 0.
sections.plainLanguage: Every envelope has a small label: which instruction sheet to use, whether it is part of a bigger piece, what is inside and how many pieces.

sections.title: Payload Data and Packing
sections.content:
Raw Vorbis packets have no fixed upper size; application profiles will likely define a limit. The text says packets range from 2-3 bytes to 8-12 kilobytes, and that the reference implementation usually produces packets below about 800 bytes except setup headers of about 4-12 kilobytes. To avoid IP fragmentation, the complete RTP packet SHOULD stay smaller than the path MTU.

Each Vorbis packet in the payload starts with a two-octet length, a network byte order integer giving the size of the following data (not counting the length field itself). The data is padded to a byte boundary. The oldest packet comes right after the headers, and later packets follow in temporal order, as RFC 3551 requires.

Any Vorbis packet smaller than the path MTU SHOULD be bundled with as many others as fit, up to 15, unless that would exceed the application's latency target.
sections.plainLanguage: Each audio chunk gets a tag saying how long it is. Small chunks share an envelope, as long as they do not make the listener wait.

sections.title: Configuration Headers
sections.content:
Vorbis has no fixed probability model. The entropy decoding, vector quantization and Huffman models, plus channel count and bit rates, form the codebooks sent as header packets before any audio. A comment header with metadata is also required by Vorbis I but is not needed for decoding. Because RTP often runs over unreliable transport, this data needs careful delivery.

The initial configuration MUST be conveyed through the session signalling channel, such as SDP with the offer/answer model (RFC 3264). Changes MAY be sent through a re-invite with new SDP or in-band. Implementations MUST support in-band updates and SHOULD support out-of-band updates. For non-chained streams, the recommended method is the Packed Configuration inside the SDP.

The Ident tells the receiver which configuration applies. If it changes and the client lacks that configuration, it MUST NOT decode the raw data until it has fetched it.

A Packed Configuration uses VDT 1. The Identification and Setup headers MUST be packed as they are, while the Comment header MAY be a dummy. A count field stores the number of following packets minus one, then length fields, then the headers in the order Identification, Comment, Setup. Numbers are stored 7 bits per byte, with the top bit flagging that more bytes follow. In-band, this payload has fragment type 0 and a packet count of 1. Out of band, the packed headers start with a 32-bit count of headers and have no payload header octet. Its media type is audio/vorbis-config.

Comment packets use VDT 2; clients MAY ignore them. If a configuration is lost, decoding is impossible, so implementations MAY re-request it or buffer payloads, and the baseline reaction SHOULD be to reset or end the RTP session.
sections.plainLanguage: The player needs a recipe book before it can play. The book comes with the call setup, and a new ticket number says when to switch to a different book.

sections.title: Fragmentation and Packet Loss
sections.content:
A payload holds either one fragment of a Vorbis packet or a whole number of complete packets. A fragment has a packet count of 0. The first fragment uses fragment type 1, later ones 2, and the final one 3. Fragments MUST follow one another with no other payload between them. All fragments keep the same RTP timestamp as the first, while the sequence number rises as normal. The text notes this affects RTCP jitter measurement.

The RFC's example splits a packet over three payloads with sequence numbers 1000, 1001 and 1002 and timestamp 12345.

Vorbis has no error correction, so loss means loss of signal. If a fragment is lost, the client MUST discard the remaining fragments and decode the incomplete packet. For example, if the first fragment is lost, the client sees fragment type 2 with count 0 and MUST drop it, and the last fragment too. If only the last one is missing, the received fragments are kept and the incomplete packet is decoded.
sections.plainLanguage: A big piece is cut into numbered parts. If the first part gets lost, the rest are useless and are thrown away.

sections.title: Media Types and SDP
sections.content:
The RFC registers the media type audio/vorbis with required parameters rate, channels and configuration (the base64 form of the packed headers), and a second type audio/vorbis-config for the packed headers themselves. The first is defined only for transfer via RTP.

In SDP, audio goes in the m= line, vorbis in a=rtpmap with rate and channels, and configuration in a=fmtp. For chained streams known in advance, each file's configuration SHOULD be passed in the configuration attribute. The clock rate MUST be a multiple of the sample rate, and a different payload number MUST be used if it changes. Implementations MUST ignore unknown parameters.

With the offer/answer model there are no negotiable parameters; all are declarative.
sections.plainLanguage: On the call setup sheet, you write what kind of audio it is, how fast it runs and attach the recipe book. Nothing is up for haggling.

sections.title: Congestion and Security
sections.content:
General RTP congestion control considerations apply. Audio can be encoded at many bit rates, so a sender can adapt to the network by changing the encoder bit rate in real time or by offering copies at different rates.

Security follows RTP (RFC 3550), base64 (RFC 4648) and URI syntax (RFC 3986). Confidentiality comes from encryption, and since compression is end-to-end, encryption may be applied to the compressed data.
sections.plainLanguage: If the road is busy, send smaller music. To keep it private, lock it before sending.

fields.name: Ident
fields.desc: Associates the data with a decoding configuration.

fields.name: F
fields.desc: Fragment type: 0 whole, 1 start, 2 continuation, 3 end.

fields.name: VDT
fields.desc: Vorbis data type: 0 raw, 1 packed configuration, 2 comment, 3 reserved.

fields.name: # pkts.
fields.desc: Number of complete packets; 0 when fragmented.

items.label: Start Fragment
items.desc: First piece of a split packet.

items.label: End Fragment
items.desc: Last piece of a split packet.

data.title: SDP for a Vorbis stream
data.code:
c=IN IP4 192.0.2.1
m=audio RTP/AVP 98
a=rtpmap:98 vorbis/44100/2
a=fmtp:98 configuration=AAAAAZ2f4g9NAh4aAXZvcmJpcwA...;
